bugs: A row edited while its push is in flight is never marked synced, and its claim is not cleared either (app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:77-79). It stays claimed and is not re-dispatched until the 15-minute abandoned-claim TTL runs out. A probe confirmed it was not re-dispatched one minute later. The change is not lost, but it reaches the storefront up to 15 minutes late. The suite's own test asserts this behaviour (StockSyncTest.php:209).

The optimistic check compares updated_at at one-second precision. An edit that lands in the same second as the row's previous updated_at matches the old value, so the row is marked synced and the edit is lost. A probe confirmed this.

failed() clears sync_started_at on every id without checking that this job still owns the claim. If the claim has expired and another run has re-claimed the rows, they can be claimed and sent a third time.
antipatterns: app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:59-60 groups rows by updated_at string and issues one pair of UPDATEs per group, up to 200 queries per 100-row job. This optimistic-lock workaround is harder to follow than snapshotting synced_at to the read time.
app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:50 packs the Retry-After parse, default and cap into a single line inside release().
app/Models/StockAllocation.php:12 makes sync_started_at, synced_at and disabled_at mass-assignable, which they don't need to be.
tests/Feature/StockSyncTest.php:13-16 has a runJob() helper that only calls handle(), which adds nothing.
tests/Feature/StockSyncTest.php:151-153 and 163-164 hand-mock the queue Job with Mockery instead of using withFakeQueueInteractions() and assertReleased().
app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:46 hardcodes the timeouts as magic numbers.
strengths: Claiming is correct: chunkById, then a re-check under lockForUpdate inside a transaction, with toBase() so updated_at is not bumped.
Scheduled with onOneServer and withoutOverlapping(5). retryUntil ends before the claim TTL, and failed() releases the claim.
Handles 429 with release(Retry-After), capped and defaulted. connectTimeout is set, and there is a sensible composite index.
Tests use describe blocks, cover readiness, batching, abandoned claims, 429, 5xx, idempotency and in-flight edits, and assert the schedule's expiresAt.

bugs: synced_at is set to the read time ($startedAt) at one-second precision. An edit in the same second as the read gives updated_at == synced_at, so the row does not count as ready and the edit is lost. A probe confirmed this. The window is narrow.

The synced and disabled UPDATEs are not wrapped in a transaction (app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:71-80). If the second one fails, for example when the response has 'missing': null and whereIn gets a TypeError (confirmed by a probe), the rows are already marked synced. The retry then finds no claimed rows, so the missing SKUs are never disabled.
failed() clears sync_started_at on every id without checking that this job still owns the claim. This is the same as impl-1, and retryUntil at 10 minutes makes it unlikely.
antipatterns: app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:67 passes json('missing', []) to whereIn without casting to an array or wrapping it in a collection.
app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:71-80 runs two related bulk updates outside DB::transaction.
tests/Feature/PushStockAllocationsTest.php:9 and StockSyncTest in impl-1 both define a global const STOCK_URL. That only works because the two suites are in separate apps.
tests/Feature/StockAllocationTest.php:44 has a redundant assertion ($fresh->id not equal to $abandoned->id).
strengths: Simple design for edits made while a push is in flight: synced_at is snapshotted to the read time and updated_at is left untouched, so a later edit stays ready on the next run without waiting for the TTL.
Claiming is correct: chunkById over select('id'), then a re-check under lockForUpdate in a transaction, with toBase() updates. Scheduled with onOneServer and withoutOverlapping.

Uses current queue attributes (Timeout, Backoff, MaxExceptions, FailOnTimeout). retryUntil is derived from CLAIM_TTL_MINUTES, failed() releases the claim, and a small retryAfter() helper handles 429 with a cap.

Tests are idiomatic Pest: withFakeQueueInteractions() with assertReleased(delay:), datasets, preventStrayRequests, and separate files for the model, command and job. They cover 429, 5xx, giving up, edits in flight, idempotency and abandoned claims.

v.rationale:
Both implementations are strong and share the same core: a chunkById pass whose claim is re-checked under lockForUpdate, toBase() so updated_at is not bumped, onOneServer and withoutOverlapping, release on 429 using Retry-After, retryUntil ending before the 15-minute claim TTL, and failed() releasing the claim. All tests pass in both (impl-2: 26, impl-1: 24).

The deciding difference is how each handles an edit made while a push is in flight. impl-2 sets synced_at to the read time, so the edited row is ready on the very next run. impl-1 uses an optimistic check on updated_at and leaves the edited row claimed. That row is not re-sent until the 15-minute TTL expires, which a probe confirmed. impl-1's version also costs more queries and is more complex.

impl-2's job tests are more modern: withFakeQueueInteractions() and assertReleased instead of Mockery mocks of the queue job. Its timeouts are named constants rather than magic numbers.

impl-2's weaknesses are smaller:
- The two final updates run outside a transaction.
- It does not guard against a null "missing" value in the response.

Both share a one-second race in which an edit can be lost.
